angle: a millionaire's normal Tuesday, from 3 angles: numbers (morning), psychology (workday), playbook (evening)
title: How Millionaires Spend a Normal Tuesday

scenes.text: Hi, I'm Ryan Rover. When you imagine a millionaire's Tuesday, you probably imagine champagne, a private jet, and a meeting on a yacht. But the research on real American millionaires paints a very different picture. Their Tuesday looks a lot like yours. The alarm, the commute, the work, the dinner. The difference is in a handful of small choices along the way. Today, we're going to walk through a normal Tuesday, hour by hour, and find twenty of those choices.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Here's a fact that changes how you picture millionaires. In Ramsey Solutions' National Study of Millionaires, a survey of more than ten thousand American millionaires, seventy nine percent said they did not receive any inheritance at all.

card.label: millionaires who inherited nothing
card.sub: Ramsey Solutions, National Study of Millionaires

scenes.short_hook: Most millionaires never got a single dollar of inheritance.

scenes.text: In that same study, the most common careers among the millionaires were things like engineer, accountant, teacher, manager and attorney. Ordinary professional jobs. Thomas Stanley found something similar decades earlier in The Millionaire Next Door. Most millionaires were self made, many owned small businesses, and many lived in normal neighborhoods. So when we look at a millionaire's Tuesday, we're mostly looking at the Tuesday of a regular person who made a lot of good small decisions, for a long time.
scenes.caption: ORDINARY JOBS

scenes.text: We'll look at this day from three angles. First, the numbers. The money decisions that happen almost automatically, from the morning coffee to the commute. Second, the psychology. How millionaires think during the day, at work and in conversations. And third, the playbook. The evening and night routines that quietly build wealth while everyone else is scrolling. Along the way, I'll point out which parts you can copy tomorrow, whatever your income.
scenes.caption: THREE ANGLES

scenes.text: Alright. It's six thirty in the morning, and the alarm just went off. Let's go.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Our sources. Millionaire profiles come from Ramsey Solutions' National Study of Millionaires and from Thomas Stanley's research. Time use data comes from the Bureau of Labor Statistics' American Time Use Survey. Some habit statistics come from author Tom Corley's Rich Habits survey, which is small and self reported, so treat those numbers as interesting, not as proof. Growth examples use a stated seven percent average yearly return, which is an illustration, not a promise. This is education, not financial advice.
scenes.caption: OUR SOURCES

scenes.text: Angle one. The numbers. The morning is where a lot of automatic money decisions happen, and millionaires have quietly set most of them up in advance.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Six thirty. Moment number one. Before the millionaire even opens their eyes, money has already moved.

card.title: The money moved before they woke up

scenes.caption: 1 OF 20
scenes.chapter: 1. The money moved before they woke up

scenes.text: On payday, a set amount goes straight from the paycheck into a retirement account, and another amount into savings or a brokerage account. They don't decide to invest each month. It just happens. In Ramsey's study, about eight in ten millionaires said they invested in their company's retirement plan. Automatic investing is the single most common thread in how ordinary people become millionaires.
scenes.caption: MONEY MOVES FIRST

scenes.text: The reason automation works so well is that it removes the daily decision. If you had to choose to invest every single month, you'd skip months. Life would get in the way. A car repair, a holiday, a sale. With automation, the default is that you invest, and you'd have to actively stop it. Behavioral economists have shown that defaults are incredibly powerful, which is why companies that automatically enroll employees in retirement plans see much higher participation.
scenes.caption: THE DEFAULT IS INVEST

scenes.text: Copy it tomorrow. Log into your payroll or bank account and set one automatic transfer for the day after payday. Start with whatever doesn't hurt, even one percent of your pay. Then put a reminder in your calendar to raise it every six months. Within a few years, you'll be investing a meaningful share of your income without ever feeling the decision.
scenes.caption: RAISE IT EVERY 6 MONTHS

scenes.text: Six forty five. Moment number two. Coffee. Usually at home.
scenes.caption: 2 OF 20

scenes.text: Let's be honest. Coffee isn't going to make or break anyone's retirement on its own. Personal finance writers have argued about the latte factor for years, and the truth is somewhere in the middle. But the habit behind it matters. Millionaires in Stanley's research tended to be deliberate about everyday spending. They didn't do everything on autopilot.
scenes.caption: COFFEE AT HOME

scenes.text: If a coffee shop drink costs around five or six dollars and you buy one every workday, that's well over one thousand dollars a year. Some people decide that's worth it, and that's fine. The point is that it's a decision. Many millionaires make coffee at home most days and enjoy the coffee shop as a treat, not a default. The same mindset applies to lunch, snacks and every small daily purchase.
scenes.caption: A TREAT, NOT A DEFAULT

scenes.text: Copy it tomorrow. Pick one daily purchase and decide on purpose how often you want it. Maybe coffee out on Fridays only. Put the money you save into your automatic investment, so you can see it grow. Spending on purpose feels much better than spending by default.
scenes.caption: SPEND ON PURPOSE

scenes.text: Seven fifteen. Moment number three. They walk out to a car that's probably several years old, and probably paid off.

card.title: A paid off car in the driveway

scenes.caption: 3 OF 20
scenes.chapter: 3. A paid off car in the driveway

scenes.text: In Stop Acting Rich, Stanley found that the median price millionaires paid for their most recent car was about thirty one thousand dollars, in a survey from the late two thousands. Ramsey's study also found that many millionaires drive mainstream brands like Toyota, Honda and Ford, and keep them for years. Meanwhile, Edmunds has reported average new car payments above seven hundred dollars a month.
scenes.caption: PAID OFF

scenes.text: Think about what no car payment means. Seven hundred dollars a month, invested at a seven percent average yearly return for ten years, grows to over one hundred twenty thousand dollars. That's the hidden power of driving a paid off car. It isn't glamorous, but each month without a payment is a month the money can work for you instead of the bank.
scenes.caption: $700 A MONTH

scenes.text: Copy it tomorrow. If you have a car loan, don't sell the car in a panic. Instead, plan to keep it for years after the last payment. When it's paid off, keep making the same payment, but to your own savings account. That fund becomes the cash for your next car.
scenes.caption: PAY YOURSELF THE PAYMENT

scenes.text: Here's that math on screen. A seven hundred dollar monthly payment, invested instead at a seven percent average yearly return, grows to roughly one hundred twenty one thousand dollars in ten years.
scenes.short_hook: This car payment is costing you a fortune.

scenes.text: Seven thirty. Moment number four. The commute. Many millionaires turn it into a classroom.
scenes.caption: 4 OF 20

scenes.text: The Bureau of Labor Statistics' American Time Use Survey and Census data show that many Americans spend close to an hour a day commuting. That's around two hundred fifty hours a year for a full time worker. Many successful people use at least part of that time for audiobooks, podcasts or language lessons.
scenes.caption: AN HOUR A DAY

scenes.text: Tom Corley's Rich Habits survey reported that most of the wealthy people he interviewed read for self improvement regularly, and that many listened to educational audio while driving. Remember, that's a small self reported survey. But the idea is sound. Two hundred fifty hours a year is like a semester of college, every year, for free.
scenes.caption: A SEMESTER A YEAR

scenes.text: Copy it tomorrow. Pick one book about money, your career or a skill you want, and listen to it during your commute this month. If you don't commute, use the time you spend doing chores or walking. One book a month is twelve books a year.
scenes.caption: 12 BOOKS A YEAR

scenes.text: Twelve noon. Moment number five. Lunch. Often brought from home.
scenes.caption: 5 OF 20

scenes.text: Buying lunch every workday can easily cost a hundred dollars or more a week in many cities. Bringing lunch most days can save thousands of dollars a year. Many millionaires do this not because they need to, but because it's how they built their wealth in the first place, and the habit stuck.
scenes.caption: LUNCH FROM HOME

scenes.text: There's a bonus. Many people who bring lunch also eat healthier, and health is one of the biggest financial assets you have. Medical costs and lost work time from health problems are expensive. A simple habit like packing lunch quietly pays off in two ways.
scenes.caption: HEALTH IS WEALTH

scenes.text: Copy it tomorrow. Cook a little extra at dinner tonight and pack it for lunch. Aim for three days a week at first. Track what you save for a month. When you see the total, it gets much easier to keep going.
scenes.caption: THREE DAYS A WEEK

scenes.text: Twelve thirty. Moment number six. A quick look at the numbers.
scenes.caption: 6 OF 20

scenes.text: Many wealthy people check their spending and accounts regularly. Not obsessively, but often enough to know where they stand. Stanley found that the millionaires he studied were far more likely than others to know exactly how much they spent each year on food, clothing and housing.
scenes.caption: A QUICK LOOK

scenes.text: Knowing your numbers changes your decisions. When you know your savings rate is twenty percent, you think twice before signing up for a new monthly payment. When you know what you spent on dining out last month, you naturally adjust. Awareness does a lot of the work that willpower can't.
scenes.caption: KNOW WHAT YOU SPEND

scenes.text: Copy it tomorrow. Put a five minute weekly money check on your calendar. Look at your balance, your spending since last week, and any upcoming bills. That's it. Five minutes a week is enough to stay in control.
scenes.caption: 5 MINUTES A WEEK

scenes.text: One fifteen. Moment number seven. The online shopping temptation.
scenes.caption: 7 OF 20

scenes.text: Office breaks are prime time for online shopping. A quick scroll, a flash sale, one click and it's on the way. Retailers know this, and many sales and emails are timed for exactly these moments.
scenes.caption: THE FLASH SALE

scenes.text: Millionaires are just as tempted, but many use a simple rule. They don't buy non essentials on impulse. They wait. A day for small items, a month for big ones. Most of the time, the urge passes. When it doesn't, they buy it without guilt, because they know they really want it.
scenes.caption: WAIT A DAY

scenes.text: Copy it tomorrow. Remove your saved card from your favorite shopping sites, and turn off one click buying. That small bit of friction gives your brain a moment to ask, do I actually need this? Then add the twenty four hour rule for anything that isn't essential.
scenes.caption: ADD FRICTION

scenes.text: That's angle one. The money moved automatically, coffee and lunch on purpose, a paid off car, a commute that teaches, a quick look at the numbers, and no impulse buys. None of these require a big salary. Now angle two. The psychology. How millionaires think during the workday.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: The middle of the day is where mindset shows up. How you handle your boss, your career, your coworkers, a sales pitch, or a bad day at the office. Millionaires aren't immune to stress or temptation. But research suggests they tend to think about time, risk and value a little differently.
scenes.caption: THE MINDSET

scenes.text: Two o'clock. Moment number eight. They think like owners, even when they're employees.
scenes.caption: 8 OF 20

scenes.text: Stanley found that a large share of millionaires were business owners, and many of the rest thought like owners at work. They asked how they could make themselves more valuable, not just how they could get through the day. Over a career, that mindset tends to lead to raises, promotions and opportunities.
scenes.caption: THINK LIKE AN OWNER

scenes.text: Thinking like an owner also changes how you see your own money. An owner asks, what will this purchase return? An employee mindset asks, can I afford the payment? Owners buy assets that grow. That simple shift in question changes thousands of decisions over a lifetime.
scenes.caption: WHAT WILL IT RETURN?

scenes.text: Copy it tomorrow. At work, ask yourself one question. What's one thing I could do this week that would make me noticeably more valuable here? Do it. And with your money, ask what a purchase will return before you ask about the payment.
scenes.caption: BE MORE VALUABLE

scenes.text: Two thirty. Moment number nine. They treat their income as their most important tool.
scenes.caption: 9 OF 20

scenes.text: Early in life, your ability to earn is usually worth far more than your savings. Raising your income by ten or twenty percent through skills or a new role can do more for your wealth than years of cutting coupons. Many self made millionaires focused hard on growing their income in their twenties and thirties.
scenes.caption: GROW THE INCOME

scenes.text: The trick is what they did with the higher income. Instead of upgrading everything, they kept their lifestyle relatively steady and invested the difference. That gap between income and spending is where wealth comes from. Earning more only helps if you keep a good part of it.
scenes.query: Graph of income and spending gap
scenes.caption: KEEP THE GAP

scenes.text: Copy it tomorrow. Look up the salary range for your role and the next role up. Identify one skill or certification that would help you get there. Spend thirty minutes a week on it. And when your next raise comes, save at least half of it.
scenes.caption: 30 MINUTES A WEEK

scenes.text: Three o'clock. Moment number ten. Someone pitches them an investment. They say no.

card.title: They say no to most pitches

scenes.caption: 10 OF 20
scenes.chapter: 10. They say no to most pitches

scenes.text: Wealthy people get a lot of pitches. Hot stocks, crypto tips, business deals, insurance products, rental schemes. Most of them are bad, some are scams. The Federal Trade Commission receives reports of billions of dollars lost to fraud every year, and investment scams are among the costliest categories.
scenes.caption: THE PITCH

scenes.text: Many millionaires follow a version of Warren Buffett's rule: only invest in what you understand. If they can't explain how the investment makes money, what it costs and how to get out, they pass. Saying no to most opportunities protects the wealth they've built.
scenes.caption: BILLIONS LOST TO FRAUD

scenes.text: Copy it tomorrow. Write these three questions on a card and keep it in your wallet. How do you make money? What are all the fees? How do I get my money out? If anyone can't answer clearly, walk away.
scenes.caption: THREE QUESTIONS

scenes.text: Let me take a short break here. If you're enjoying this walk through a millionaire's Tuesday, please subscribe to Ryan Rover Money. It's free, and it tells me to make more videos like this one. Okay, it's three thirty in the afternoon. Back to the office.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Three thirty. Moment number eleven. A coworker shows off a new car. The millionaire doesn't care.

card.title: They don't keep up with coworkers

scenes.caption: 11 OF 20
scenes.chapter: 11. They don't keep up with coworkers

scenes.text: Workplaces are full of quiet status competition. Cars in the parking lot, watches, vacations, clothes. Stanley described how many high earners felt pressure to look successful, which kept them from building real wealth. Many quiet millionaires simply opted out of that game.
scenes.caption: THE PARKING LOT

scenes.text: Opting out isn't about judging anyone. It's about knowing your own goals. Every dollar spent on looking successful is a dollar that can't buy freedom later. Millionaires often care more about owning their time than about impressing the people in the next cubicle.
scenes.caption: OPT OUT

scenes.text: Copy it tomorrow. Next time you feel the pull to match someone else's purchase, ask: does this move me toward my own goals? If not, let it go. You're running your own race.
scenes.caption: RUN YOUR OWN RACE

scenes.text: Four o'clock. Moment number twelve. A market headline says stocks dropped. They barely react.
scenes.caption: 12 OF 20

scenes.text: Market drops are normal. Broad stock markets have fallen significantly many times in history, and have historically recovered over long periods, though there are no guarantees and recovery can take years. Millionaires who built wealth through investing usually learned to ignore daily noise.
scenes.caption: STOCKS DROPPED
scenes.short_hook: Why millionaires barely react when stocks drop.

scenes.text: Their mindset is measured in decades, not days. A bad Tuesday on the market is a footnote in a thirty year plan. Many keep investing through drops, which means they buy more shares when prices are lower. That patience is one of the biggest advantages ordinary investors have.
scenes.caption: THINK IN DECADES

scenes.text: Copy it tomorrow. Turn off stock price notifications on your phone. Check your investments once a month or once a quarter, not once a day. And decide now what you'll do in a crash, which for most long term investors is: keep investing.
scenes.caption: TURN OFF THE NOISE

scenes.text: Five thirty. Moment number thirteen. A walk, a run or the gym.
scenes.caption: 13 OF 20

scenes.text: Corley's survey reported that most of the wealthy people he interviewed exercised regularly. Again, a small survey. But the link between health and wealth shows up elsewhere too. Good health means fewer medical bills, fewer missed workdays, and more years of earning and enjoying your money.
scenes.caption: THE DAILY WALK

scenes.text: Exercise also helps with stress, and stress is expensive. Stressed people tend to make more impulsive money decisions. A daily walk is one of the cheapest investments you can make, with returns in energy, mood and focus.
scenes.caption: FEWER MEDICAL BILLS

scenes.text: Copy it tomorrow. Take a twenty minute walk after work. No equipment, no gym membership needed. If you like company, invite a friend or family member. Health is a form of wealth that money can't buy back.
scenes.caption: 20 MINUTES

scenes.text: That's angle two. Owners, not just employees. Income as a tool. No to most pitches. No status games. Decades, not days. And health as wealth. Now angle three. The playbook. The evening and night, where a lot of the real wealth building happens.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: The evening is when most people are tired and on autopilot. That's exactly why it's such a powerful time to build better habits. A few small routines between six p.m. and bedtime can add up to a completely different financial life over ten or twenty years.
scenes.query: City at dusk lights coming on
scenes.caption: THE EVENING

scenes.text: Six thirty. Moment number fourteen. Dinner at home, with family.
scenes.caption: 14 OF 20

scenes.text: Restaurant meals and delivery add up fast. Many millionaires eat most dinners at home. Not because they can't afford restaurants, but because home dinners are cheaper, healthier, and give them time with the people they care about.
scenes.caption: DINNER AT HOME

scenes.text: Dinner is also when many families talk about money. Stanley found that millionaires often taught their kids about money early, including saving, budgeting and the value of work. Those conversations can shape a child's financial habits for life.
scenes.caption: TEACHING KIDS

scenes.text: Copy it tomorrow. Plan four home dinners this week. Keep them simple. And at one of them, ask a money question. What would you do with a hundred dollars? How do you think people get rich? It's a great way to start the conversation.
scenes.caption: FOUR DINNERS A WEEK

scenes.text: Seven thirty. Moment number fifteen. The TV gap.
scenes.caption: 15 OF 20

scenes.text: According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics' American Time Use Survey, watching TV is the top leisure activity for Americans, at close to three hours a day on average. That's around twenty hours a week. Add social media and phones, and many evenings simply disappear.
scenes.caption: 3 HOURS OF TV A DAY
scenes.short_hook: Americans spend about three hours a day on this.

scenes.text: Warren Buffett has said he spends a large part of each day reading. Bill Gates is famous for reading dozens of books a year. You don't need to match them. But swapping even thirty minutes of TV for reading or learning, five nights a week, adds up to more than one hundred twenty hours a year.
scenes.caption: READ FIRST

scenes.text: Copy it tomorrow. Set a simple rule. Thirty minutes of reading or learning before any TV. Keep a book on the couch where the remote usually sits. It's a small change with a surprisingly big payoff over the years.
scenes.caption: 30 MINUTES

scenes.text: Eight fifteen. Moment number sixteen. Working on something of their own.
scenes.caption: 16 OF 20

scenes.text: Many millionaires built their wealth through a business, and many started that business on the side, in the evenings. A side project can be a small online store, freelance work, a skill they're developing, or a rental property they manage.
scenes.caption: SOMETHING OF YOUR OWN

scenes.text: Not every side project becomes a business. But even small ones build skills, create a second income stream, and give you options if your main job changes. And the income from a side project can go straight into investments, speeding everything up.
scenes.caption: A SECOND STREAM

scenes.text: Copy it tomorrow. Pick one evening a week for a side project. Start with something low cost that uses a skill you already have. Track every dollar you earn from it and invest most of it.
scenes.caption: ONE EVENING A WEEK

scenes.text: Nine o'clock. Moment number seventeen. A quick money conversation with their partner.
scenes.caption: 17 OF 20

scenes.text: Money is one of the most common sources of conflict in relationships. Couples who talk about money regularly, set shared goals and make big decisions together tend to have fewer fights about it. Stanley found that many millionaires described their spouse as a key partner in building wealth.
scenes.caption: ON THE SAME TEAM

scenes.text: It doesn't have to be a big meeting. A few minutes to check in. Any big expenses coming up? Are we on track with savings? Anything we want to change? Small regular conversations prevent big blowups.
scenes.caption: SHARED GOALS

scenes.text: Copy it tomorrow. Pick one evening a week for a ten minute money check in with your partner. Keep it positive. Start with a win, then talk about what's coming up. If you're single, do it with yourself, in a notebook.
scenes.caption: 10 MINUTES A WEEK

scenes.text: Nine thirty. Moment number eighteen. Planning tomorrow.
scenes.caption: 18 OF 20

scenes.text: Many successful people spend a few minutes each evening planning the next day. What are the three most important things? What's for lunch? What's on the calendar? This simple habit reduces stress and helps avoid expensive last minute decisions.
scenes.query: To do list on desk at night
scenes.caption: PLAN TOMORROW

scenes.text: Last minute decisions are often expensive ones. The rushed breakfast bought on the way to work, the forgotten bill that becomes a late fee, the unplanned dinner that turns into delivery. A little planning the night before prevents a lot of small, costly mistakes.
scenes.caption: LAST MINUTE COSTS

scenes.text: Copy it tomorrow. Before bed, write down three priorities for tomorrow and pack your lunch. Five minutes. You'll wake up with a plan instead of a scramble.
scenes.caption: THREE PRIORITIES

scenes.text: Ten o'clock. Moment number nineteen. A moment of gratitude.
scenes.caption: 19 OF 20

scenes.text: Many wealthy people talk about the idea of enough. Knowing what's enough for you protects you from endless spending, because there's always a bigger house or a newer car. Researchers who study well being have found that gratitude is linked with greater life satisfaction.
scenes.query: Person writing in journal at night
scenes.caption: GRATITUDE

scenes.text: Gratitude also fights the envy that drives so much spending. When you appreciate what you have, you need less to feel good. That's not just good for your mood. It's good for your bank account.
scenes.caption: WHAT IS ENOUGH?

scenes.text: Copy it tomorrow. Before bed, write down three things you're grateful for that don't cost money. It takes two minutes, and over time it changes how you think about wanting more.
scenes.caption: THREE THINGS

scenes.text: Ten thirty. Moment number twenty. Lights out.
scenes.caption: 20 OF 20

scenes.text: Sleep sounds like it has nothing to do with money. But tired people make worse decisions, including financial ones. Research has linked sleep deprivation with poorer judgment and more impulsive choices. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says about a third of American adults don't get enough sleep.
scenes.caption: LIGHTS OUT

scenes.text: A good night's sleep helps you focus at work, resist late night online shopping, and handle stress without spending to cope. Many successful people protect their sleep as carefully as their savings.
scenes.caption: TIRED DECISIONS

scenes.text: Copy it tomorrow. Set a consistent bedtime and put your phone away thirty minutes before it. Late night scrolling is when a lot of impulse shopping happens. Protect your sleep, and you protect your wallet.
scenes.caption: PHONE AWAY

scenes.text: So what does one Tuesday really add up to? On its own, not much. That's the secret.
scenes.caption: RYAN
scenes.chapter: What one Tuesday adds up to

scenes.text: One Tuesday of packing lunch saves a few dollars. One evening of reading teaches you a few pages. One automatic transfer moves a small amount. On their own, these moments look meaningless. But a year has fifty two Tuesdays, and a career has about two thousand of them. Repeat those small choices two thousand times, and the result is a completely different life.
scenes.caption: 2,000 TUESDAYS

scenes.text: Here's the money side. If these habits free up five hundred dollars a month, and you invest it at a seven percent average yearly return, after thirty years that's roughly six hundred ten thousand dollars.

And that's just the money you saved. Add the raises from the skills you built in all those commutes, the side income from those evenings, and the health from those walks, and it's easy to see how ordinary people end up as quiet millionaires. Not through one big moment. Through thousands of small ones.
scenes.caption: THOUSANDS OF SMALL MOMENTS

scenes.text: Does this kind of Tuesday really make millionaires? Let me tell you about a few real people.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Ronald Read worked as a gas station attendant and later as a janitor in Brattleboro, Vermont. He lived simply, drove an old car and was known for his modest habits. When he died in twenty fourteen, people discovered he had built a fortune of around eight million dollars, mostly by buying shares of well known companies and holding them for decades. He left millions to his local hospital and library.
scenes.caption: RONALD READ
scenes.short_hook: A janitor quietly built an eight million dollar fortune.

scenes.text: Grace Groner was a secretary at Abbott Laboratories near Chicago. In nineteen thirty five, she bought three shares of Abbott stock for one hundred eighty dollars. She never sold. She reinvested the dividends, lived in a small one bedroom house, and bought her clothes at rummage sales. When she died in twenty ten, her stock was worth about seven million dollars, which she left to her college, Lake Forest College.
scenes.caption: GRACE GRONER

scenes.text: And then there's Warren Buffett, one of the richest people in the world, who still lives in the Omaha house he bought in nineteen fifty eight. In the documentary Becoming Warren Buffett, he described stopping at McDonald's on his drive to work and choosing breakfast based on how the market was doing that day, spending just a few dollars.
scenes.caption: WARREN BUFFETT

scenes.text: None of these people had a glamorous Tuesday. They had a patient one. They spent less than they earned, invested the difference in things they understood, and gave time the chance to work. Their stories are extreme, but the habits behind them are available to anyone.
scenes.caption: A PATIENT TUESDAY

scenes.text: Now picture the other Tuesday. The alarm goes off late. No time for breakfast, so it's a drive through on the way to work in a car with a seven hundred dollar payment. Lunch is bought. A flash sale gets a quick click. The evening is three hours of TV and scrolling, a delivery dinner, and a late night of online shopping. The paycheck is gone before the next one arrives.
scenes.caption: THE OTHER TUESDAY

scenes.text: Nobody on that Tuesday is doing anything terrible. That's what makes it so common. Each choice is reasonable on its own. But two thousand of those Tuesdays lead to a very different place than two thousand of the millionaire's Tuesdays. The difference was never one big decision. It was always the small ones.
scenes.caption: TWO DIFFERENT PLACES

scenes.text: The good news is you don't have to switch everything at once. Try changing just three moments. One from the morning, one from the workday, one from the evening. Next month, add three more. Within a year, your Tuesday can look a lot like the millionaire's, whatever your income is today.
scenes.caption: THREE MOMENTS AT A TIME

scenes.text: A normal Tuesday is built on daily habits. But millionaires also have a few moments that happen once a month or once a year. Here are the big ones.
scenes.caption: RYAN
scenes.chapter: Bonus: the once a month moments

scenes.text: Once a month, many wealthy people do a money review. They look at net worth, savings rate and any changes in spending. It takes maybe half an hour. They ask simple questions. Did we spend what we planned? Did anything surprise us? Is there a subscription or fee we can cut? Is our savings rate going up or down?
scenes.caption: THE MONTHLY REVIEW

scenes.text: Once a year, they do a bigger checkup. Insurance policies, beneficiaries on retirement accounts, the investment mix, and goals for the next year. Many also review their tax situation before the year ends, looking for things like maxing out retirement contributions. These annual reviews catch problems before they become expensive.
scenes.caption: THE YEARLY CHECKUP

scenes.text: And whenever they get a raise, they follow a simple rule. Before any lifestyle upgrade, they increase their automatic saving. Many save at least half of every raise. That single habit is one of the most powerful ways to build wealth, because your lifestyle never catches up with your income, and the gap keeps growing year after year.
scenes.caption: SAVE HALF THE RAISE

scenes.text: Finally, many give. Studies of wealthy households, and Stanley's research, found that many millionaires give regularly to charity, their church, or causes they care about. Giving keeps money in perspective. It's a reminder that money is a tool for a good life, not the goal itself.
scenes.caption: GIVING

scenes.text: A word of warning. When people see a routine like this, they often try to copy everything on day one. Up at five, no coffee out, no TV, side project every night, reading an hour a day. By Friday, they've quit. Big overnight changes rarely last. Small changes that stack up over months usually do.
scenes.caption: DON'T COPY EVERYTHING AT ONCE

scenes.text: The second mistake is copying the look instead of the habit. Buying a fancy planner, an expensive water bottle and a gym membership feels like progress, but it's just more spending. The habits on this list are almost all free. Start with the free ones.
scenes.caption: COPY THE HABIT, NOT THE LOOK

scenes.text: And the third mistake is comparing your chapter one with someone else's chapter twenty. A fifty five year old millionaire's Tuesday is the result of thirty years of habits. Yours is just getting started. Judge your progress against last year's version of you, not against someone further down the road.
scenes.caption: YOUR CHAPTER ONE

scenes.text: Question one. Do all millionaires live like this? No. Some are flashy, some inherited their money, and some got lucky. But research like Stanley's and Ramsey's suggests that the typical American millionaire is self made and lives below their means, much like the Tuesday we just walked through.
scenes.caption: ALL MILLIONAIRES?

scenes.text: Question two. I work nights or shifts. Does this still apply? Absolutely. The clock times don't matter. What matters are the moments. Automatic saving, food on purpose, learning while you travel, a daily walk, time with family, and protecting your sleep. Fit them into your own schedule.
scenes.caption: SHIFT WORK?

scenes.text: Question three. How long does it take to become a millionaire this way? It depends on your income, your savings rate and market returns, which aren't guaranteed. Ramsey's study reported that the average age at which those millionaires reached a million dollars was around forty nine. For most, it was a long, steady journey, not a sprint.
scenes.caption: HOW LONG IT TAKES

scenes.text: Question four. Should I wake up at five like some successful people? Only if it suits you. There's no magic in the hour itself. What matters is having some time each day that you control, whether that's early morning, lunch, or late evening. Use that time for things that grow, like learning, exercise, or a side project.
scenes.caption: UP AT FIVE?

scenes.text: Question five. What if my partner doesn't want to change? Start with yourself and share results, not lectures. Bring lunch, track what you save, and show the number after a month. Progress is persuasive. And when you do talk, focus on goals you both want, like a vacation, a house, or less stress.
scenes.caption: IF YOUR PARTNER WON'T CHANGE

scenes.text: Question six. Which single moment matters most? If you only copy one, copy the first one. Money moved automatically before you wake up. It's the habit behind almost every quiet millionaire story, it takes ten minutes to set up, and after that it works every single Tuesday without asking anything of you. Every other moment on this list makes it stronger, but that one is the foundation.
scenes.caption: THE ONE THAT MATTERS MOST

scenes.text: Quick recap. Angle one, the numbers, the morning. Money moved automatically, coffee at home, a paid off car, a commute that teaches, lunch from home, knowing their numbers, and no impulse buys.
scenes.caption: THE MORNING: 1 TO 7

scenes.text: Angle two, the psychology, the workday. Thinking like owners, treating income as a tool, saying no to most pitches, ignoring status games, thinking in decades, and protecting their health.
scenes.caption: THE WORKDAY: 8 TO 13

scenes.text: Angle three, the playbook, the evening. Dinner at home, screens off and books on, a side project, money talk with their partner, planning tomorrow, gratitude, and sleep.
scenes.caption: THE EVENING: 14 TO 20

scenes.text: Here's the thing I love about this. You don't need a lucky break, a rich family or a genius idea to live a millionaire's Tuesday. You just need a few good defaults, repeated for a long time, with the patience to let them work while everybody else is chasing something faster. Tomorrow is a normal day for you, too. Pick three moments from this video and try them. If you want the full plan for turning ordinary days into real wealth, it's in my playbook, linked in the description. Tell me in the comments which moment you're starting with. I'm Ryan Rover. See you in the next one.
scenes.caption: RYAN
